entry.evidence: The most important innovation used in this research, as emphasized in the article, is the extraction of unique cross-sections for 414 different waterways

steps.action: The authors review published GSSHA applications, including Sharif et al. (2010), cited as finding that model accuracy falls as grid size grows.
steps.quote: Observed discharge was compared to hydrographs obtained from the accuracy of model decreases by increasing the grid sizes.

steps.action: From the review, the authors pose a gap. One-dimensional diffusive-wave routing and waterway cross-sections in large GSSHA watersheds have received little attention, and the authors ask how these setup choices affect results.
steps.quote: less attention has been paid to one-dimensional hydraulic routing of flow by diffusive wave method in the GSSHA model

steps.action: The authors adopt the published GSSHA formulation (Downer et al.): Green-Ampt infiltration, Manning-based 1-D channel and 2-D overland diffusive-wave routing, and the ADE/ADEPC explicit schemes.
steps.quote: The Green-Ampt (GA) equation has been used as an infiltration model in the current study.

steps.action: The authors extract unique cross-sections for all 414 waterways (drainage area > 5 km2) from the DEM and define three routing states: main river and tributaries, all streams > 5 km2, and no streams. Sample sections are in Fig. 4.
steps.quote: the cross-sections of all 414 waterways of the Karavandar River hydrographic network are uniquely extracted from DEM

steps.action: The authors assemble the available data: daily and peak discharges at the Daman outlet station (no flood hydrographs) and 24-h rainfall from five rain gauges, which they judge spatially insufficient.
steps.quote: Daman hydrometric station has 45 years of daily and peak discharges but no flood hydrographs.

steps.action: The authors build the base model: a 200 m grid of about 86,200 cells on the 12.5 m ALOS PALSAR DEM. Infiltration and roughness parameters come from geological maps and cluster analysis of satellite images, Manning's n is a uniform 0.035, and rainfall is interpolated by IDW (§3 ¶1, ¶3–5).
steps.quote: includes a square grid containing about 86,200 square cells of 200 m

steps.action: The authors calibrate the base model against outlet peak discharges of two flood events (no hydrographs are available, §3 ¶1). The 10 s time step is set by trial and error.
steps.quote: the base model was calibrated for the two flood events

steps.action: The authors validate the calibrated model on three other flood events. No error statistics or observed peak values are reported.
steps.quote: validated for three other major flood events

steps.action: The authors design five spatially uniform 24-h storms (60, 65, 70, 75, 80 mm), so that setup changes are compared under identical meteorological forcing.
steps.quote: The main goal in choosing the uniform spatial distribution of design storms is to compare the topographic, geometric, and physical changes of the base model

steps.action: Preliminary simulations show that time of concentration varies with storm magnitude and watershed complexity, contrasting with lumped models.
steps.quote: the concentration–time of the watershed in flood events with different peak discharges is fully variable

steps.action: The authors replace the 12.5 m ALOS PALSAR DEM with the 30 m ASTER GDEM and rerun the January 2008 event and the five design storms.
steps.quote: was replaced by the USA Aster GDEM with a spatial resolution of 30 m

steps.action: The authors compare peak discharges between the two DEMs (Tables 3–4, Figs. 13–14). Base-model peaks are slightly lower (< 4%), and they conclude the 30 m DEM introduces no practical error.
steps.quote: these results confirm that using a topographic model with a lower spatial resolution does not have practical errors in the accuracy of the GSSHA model

steps.action: The authors build a second model that routes all streams with drainage area > 5 km2 using the extracted cross-sections, and run the five design storms.
steps.quote: Another GSSHA model was provided for the streams and waterways containing the drainage area greater than 5 km2.

steps.action: The authors compare peaks with the base model (Table 5, Figs. 15–16). Peaks rise strongly with stream density (44–57% per §4 ¶2), and time to peak shortens.
steps.quote: by increasing the density of waterways in the GSSHA model, the peak flood increased significantly

steps.action: The authors run the five design storms with no 1-D diffusive-wave channel routing.
steps.quote: the simulation was performed without 1-D diffusion wave hydraulic routing

steps.action: The authors compare with the base model (Table 6, Fig. 17). Without routing, peaks are far lower (9% of base at 60 mm, 37% at 80 mm), and the gap is larger for small storms.
steps.quote: The differences in results were more significant for the storms with low cumulative depths.

steps.action: The authors rebuild the model at 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300 m cell sizes and run the January 2008 event and the five design storms.
steps.quote: five different cell sizes were adapted to 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300 m in modeling the geometry of the watershed

steps.action: The authors compare peaks across cell sizes (Tables 7–12, Figs. 18–23). They judge 100–200 m close to each other and 250–300 m clearly different.
steps.quote: These results indicate that using a solution grid with a cell size of more than 200 m in GSSHA models can lead to significant errors

steps.action: The authors vary cell size and stream density jointly, running the all-streams scenario on the 100 m grid.
steps.quote: Sensitivity analysis for simultaneous effects of cell size and stream density was also investigated.

steps.action: The authors compare the 100 m results (Table 13, Fig. 24). Sensitivity to stream density is smaller at the finer grid.
steps.quote: by reducing the cell size, the sensitivity of the model to the stream density decreases

steps.action: The authors recommend grids of 200 m or less. They note that smaller cells may improve calibration but sharply raise run time (§3.3 ¶3).
steps.quote: it is suggested to limit the solution grids with cell sizes less than 200 m

steps.action: The authors keep the sensitivity findings as conclusions with numbers: DEM < 4%, stream density 44–57%, and grids above 200 m giving significant errors.
steps.quote: the peak discharge of flood increases significantly (44–57%) compared with the corresponding values

tree.answer: Sensitivity of simulated GSSHA flood peaks to model setup (DEM, grid size, stream density) in a large data-poor watershed
Only outlet peak discharges are observed (no hydrographs); the model is calibrated to them
Characterize how setup choices change GSSHA peak discharge, using new cross-section extraction
None; no predictions differ across rivals
Conditions set in simulation: uniform design storms and swapped DEM, grid and routing domain
The claims are the variation results themselves; no check against observations of which setup is more accurate
Kept: 30 m DEM acceptable, stream density strongly affects peaks, grids ≤ 200 m recommended

end.claim: For the Karvandar watershed, GSSHA peak discharge changes little with DEM resolution (12.5 m vs 30 m, < 4%), rises 44–57% when all waterways > 5 km2 are routed, and is stable for grid cells up to 200 m but not at 250–300 m.

decisive_move.sentence: The deliberate swaps of DEM, routing domain and cell size, enabled by the extracted cross-sections for 414 waterways, produce every headline number; without them there is no claim.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis directed data acquisition. Existing gauge and discharge records and public DEMs were used (§2.5 ¶2, §3 ¶3, §3.1 ¶1). The main claims compare model variants with each other, not with observations, and no accuracy threshold was fixed beforehand. Statements such as 'no practical errors' (§3.1 ¶1) and 'significant errors' above 200 m (§3.3 ¶1) are judged after the runs. Calibration and validation are on peak discharge only, with no reported metrics (§3 ¶1, ¶6). Nothing was fixed before the data.

imports.item: Manning equation as head-discharge relation for channel and overland flow
Explicit finite-volume Alternating Direction Explicit (ADE) and predictor-corrector (ADEPC) schemes
Cluster analysis of satellite images to assign land-use and roughness parameters
Inverse distance weighted (IDW) interpolation of gauge rainfall onto the solution grid

limits:
No review file or earlier version was supplied, so only the final-paper sequence is coded.

Calibration and validation (§3 ¶6): no observed peaks, error metrics or calibrated parameter values are reported. Validation is coded as a replication check, but its outcome is not shown.

Accuracy is never measured. 'Accuracy' and 'errors' in §3.1 ¶1 and §3.3 ¶1 mean disagreement with the base model, not with observations. Which stream density or grid is closer to reality is not tested (inference).

The grid-size claim is weakly supported by the paper's own tables (inference from Tables 8–12):
- The 200 m base model gives the lowest peak at every design storm.
- At 60 mm, 100 m and 200 m differ by about 14%, and 300 m is closer to 100 m than 200 m is.
- The '< 15 and 0.7%' and 'about 20 and 12%' figures in §4 ¶2 are not traceable to a stated calculation.

Inconsistencies in figures and text:
- The Fig. 18 legend shows only four grids, with no 300 m (PDF p. 16).
- The Fig. 17 caption says 'six' floods where five were run (PDF p. 14).
- Fig. 9 shows Thiessen polygons while the text says rainfall was interpolated by IDW (§3 ¶1).
- The text announces 'four scenarios' (§3 ¶9) but reports three sections plus a joint test.

Methods not described: how the cross-sections were extracted (spacing, algorithm), which of the ADE or ADEPC schemes was used, and Green-Ampt versus GAR (both described, §2.1 ¶4).

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Variable time of concentration (§3 ¶8): observation from simulation, untested (status none).
- Reduced stream-density sensitivity at 100 m (§3.3 ¶2): capability_characterized, single comparison.
- 'Smaller cells can improve model calibration' (§3.3 ¶3): asserted, not shown (status none).

Coding choices:
- Entry coded capability, because the paper presents the cross-section extraction as its central innovation. A 'problem' entry (§1 ¶5 gap) is a defensible alternative.
- Composition none_fits: this is a one-case model-sensitivity study. It has no rivals, no crucial test, no repeated natural cases and no phenomenon-establishing exploration.

disagreements.target: Widespread use of the Muskingum routing method (Farzin et al. 2018; Node Farahani et al. 2018; Farahani et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: The paper asserts the diffusive wave approach is highly accurate and can route through pits and adverse slopes, but tests no comparison.
disagreements.quote: the diffusive wave approach has high accuracy

disagreements.target: Lumped and semi-distributed hydrological models (fixed watershed concentration time)
disagreements.support: Preliminary GSSHA design-storm runs show time to peak shifting with storm depth and watershed complexity; no lumped model is run for comparison.
disagreements.quote: unlike the lumped and semi-distributed hydrological models, the concentration–time of the watershed in flood events with different peak discharges is fully variable

disagreements.target: Rawls et al. (1982) soil-texture-based infiltration parameter values
disagreements.support: The paper states the values are uncertain and weakly correlated with texture, yet uses them as initial estimates; no evidence offered.
disagreements.quote: These values have great uncertainty and low correlation with textural classification and soil texture.
